Plowers
PLOW-urz
n. pl. (those who plough; in Psalm 129, the oppressors who made long furrows on Israel's back)
From Old English plog, a plough. At Psalm 129:3 it renders a Hebrew participle from charash, to cut in or engrave, used of both ploughing and devising.

Biblical Definition

Psalm 129 is one of the Songs of degrees and it opens with a nation looking back at its own scars: Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth, may Israel now say — and then the image: The plowers plowed upon my back: they made long their furrows. A ploughed back is a flogged back, the weals running parallel like furrows in a field, and the phrase they made long their furrows means they did not stop at the end of a row. The figure is agricultural and the reality is a whip.

The psalm does not linger on the injury. The next line is the turn, and it is only eight words: The LORD is righteous: he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked. The cords are the plough traces; God cuts the harness, and the ploughing stops. Isaiah takes the same image up to say what no Israelite in Psalm 129 could have guessed — that the LORD would take the furrows on Himself: he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. The back that was ploughed at the pillar in Jerusalem is the one that ends the ploughing, and the healing runs the other way down the same furrows.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): those who plow; persons who turn up the soil with a plow.

expand to see more

PLOWER, n. One that plows land; a cultivator of the soil.

PLOW, v.t. To turn up, break or divide the soil with a plow; to furrow.

FURROW, n. A trench in the earth made by a plow; a long narrow trench or channel.

SCOURGE, n. A whip; a lash consisting of a strap or cord; an instrument of punishment.

AFFLICT, v.t. To give to the body or mind pain which is continued or of some permanence; to grieve or distress.

Key Scripture

Psalm 129:3 — "The plowers plowed upon my back: they made long their furrows."

Psalm 129:1 — "Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth, may Israel now say:"

Psalm 129:4 — "The LORD is righteous: he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked."

Isaiah 53:5 — "But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed."

Modern Corruption

Suffering under persecution is either romanticized or explained away, when the Psalms simply record it, name God as righteous, and wait for Him to cut the traces.

expand to see more

Psalm 129 does something the modern instinct finds difficult: it states a long history of oppression in one line, refuses to dwell on it, and moves immediately to a confession about God's character. The LORD is righteous. Not the LORD will explain, not this will make sense later — He is righteous, and He has cut the cords. The psalm neither denies the furrows nor builds an identity on them, and a church tempted to make grievance its permanent posture should notice how quickly the Songs of degrees move off the subject.

The christological reading is not an allegorical stretch but the plain progression of Scripture's own imagery. Isaiah 53 takes the same picture of a torn back and assigns it to the Servant, and the Gospels record the scourging in a sentence so brief it is nearly missed. With his stripes we are healed uses the furrow image for the healing itself: the wounds are the channel. Israel's cry in Psalm 129 is answered not by God preventing the ploughing but by God taking it, which is the shape of nearly every promise in the Old Testament when it comes due.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew charash (H2790), to plough, to engrave, to devise; maanith (H4618), a furrow; aboth (H5688), cords or plough traces.

expand to see more

Hebrew charash (H2790) — to cut in, to plough, and also to devise mischief; the same verb for both.

Hebrew maanith (H4618) — a furrow; the long rows made on the back.

Hebrew aboth (H5688) — cords, ropes, the traces of a plough; cut asunder by the LORD.

Hebrew tsaddiq (H6662) — righteous; the psalm's one-word verdict on God.

Hebrew chaburah (H2250) — a stripe, a weal; with his stripes we are healed.

Usage

"“The plowers plowed upon my back” — an agricultural figure for a whip."

"“he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked” — the harness cut, the ploughing stopped."

"“with his stripes we are healed” — the furrows taken, and running the other way."
